An independent chronological reconstruction

Residual Continuum

What if we read climate data, archaeology, and global memory traditions as a single coherent sequence? No proof, only coherence measured honestly.
Coherence is the measure, not final demonstration.
Chronological exploration

Timeline

What we observe: What we observe: The Holocene is not an isolated stable interval but the terminal state of a long conditioning. Four background conditions are measurable and not seriously disputed: free atmospheric oxygen at approximately 21 per cent by volume; a hydrologic cycle that returns precipitation to continental interiors on annual cycles; a geomagnetic field that reduces the ionizing-radiation dose at the surface by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an unshielded body, though that reduction varies with latitude, altitude and solar activity and no single figure describes it; and soils deep enough to hold water and nutrients between rains. Each has a long and uneven history. Oxygenation is conventionally placed near 2.4 Ga on the disappearance of mass-independent sulfur isotope fractionation from sedimentary sulfides, but that transition marks the loss of an anoxic signature rather than the attainment of modern concentrations, which most reconstructions place hundreds of millions of years later and with wide error.

The narrowness of the envelope is best resolved in ice. The Vostok record across roughly 420 ka and its extension to about 800 ka at EPICA Dome C place interglacial carbon dioxide between about 260 and 300 ppm through the late Pleistocene [Petit et al. 1999; Lüthi et al. 2008]. Two caveats travel with those numbers. Gas is trapped well below the surface of the firn, so the air is younger than the ice enclosing it by an offset that at low-accumulation East Antarctic sites runs to centuries or millennia; and the amplitude of the carbon dioxide signal is far better constrained than its phasing against temperature in the same core. Reported as an envelope, the figures are robust. Read as a sequence of cause and effect, they carry the full offset uncertainty.

Soil is the youngest of the conditions. Alluvial sequences in Mesopotamia, the Nile valley and the Indus record accumulation through the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene, in the same millennia as the earliest cultivation experiments — a coincidence of timing rather than an established dependency, since the warming and sea-level history that built those floodplains also shaped the settlement pattern that used them. The arable fraction of ice-free land is often given as roughly an eighth, following standard land-cover classes, but any such figure depends on where the classification places marginal, irrigated and degraded ground. It is a convention rather than a measurement, and we do not treat it as one.

What remains debated: What remains debated: whether early Holocene stability is anomalous. Greenland δ¹⁸O variance in the Holocene is low against the last glacial, and the comparison with Marine Isotope Stage 11c has been used to argue that at least one earlier interglacial was similarly quiet [Tzedakis et al. 2012]. The comparison is not clean: orbital configurations differ, the older intervals are more thinly resolved, and low variance in one high-latitude archive is not global stability — the Holocene itself contains the 8.2 ka cooling and a series of smaller rapid changes. A second question concerns whether Pleistocene human activity, principally burning and pressure on large herbivores, helped maintain the open mosaics later farmed [Boivin et al. 2016]. The difficulty there is separating an anthropogenic signal from a climatic one within the same vegetation record.

Reading: Reading: Deep Time in this reconstruction is preparation, and the word does interpretive work the evidence does not do by itself. What is measurable is conditioning: a sequence of states each of which narrows the range of what can follow. What is not measurable is direction. The inference from suitability to intent is unavailable in principle, because the observation is made from inside the only history that produced observers — a selection effect, not an argument for or against design. We therefore hold the two apart. Coherence is high for the mechanisms, which are independently replicated across ice, sediment and rock, and it is absent for teleology, which is not a claim these archives can bear. The value of the era to what follows is comparative. It establishes the background against which the discontinuities of the terminal Pleistocene register as discontinuities at all.

Source anchors: Petit et al. 1999 Nature (Vostok, 420 ka); Lüthi et al. 2008 Nature (carbon dioxide to 800 ka); Tzedakis et al. 2012 (MIS 11 as Holocene analogue); Boivin et al. 2016 Science (anthropogenic niche construction)

paleoclimatologyplanetaryhabitability
Tier 1 — ice cores, sediment cores, pedogenesis models. Uncertainty low for mechanisms, moderate for timing thresholds; teleology falls outside the evidence entirely.

What we observe: What we observe: Skeletal anatomy consistent with modern humans is present in Africa well before the behavioural record thickens. Jebel Irhoud is placed near 300 ka by thermoluminescence on burnt flint and Omo Kibish in the 200 ka range by argon dating of bracketing tuffs; both figures carry uncertainties of tens of millennia, and both depend on the stratigraphic association between the dated material and the fossils, which has been argued in each case. What intensifies later is not anatomy but a class of behaviour returning no immediate calories: pigment prepared and applied, geometric marking, ornament made from shell carried far inland, and — inferentially, from the organisation of the artefacts themselves — language with recursive structure. Engraved ochre at Blombos around 75 ka and marked ostrich eggshell at Diepkloof around 60 ka are among the earliest secure instances [Henshilwood et al. 2002].

Whether that thickening is a change in behaviour or a change in the record is an old question and not a settled one. McBrearty and Brooks argued that the apparent threshold is partly an artefact of unequal excavation: African Middle Stone Age deposits have been sampled far less intensively than European Upper Palaeolithic ones, and each new African excavation has tended to push markers earlier. Figurative painting at Chauvet near 37 ka is late in this sequence rather than initial, and its radiocarbon determinations are on charcoal whose relation to individual images is not uniform across the cave. The defensible summary is that the package is real, that its assembly looks staggered rather than instantaneous, and that its apparent onset has moved with sampling effort in one direction only.

Origin traditions across unrelated language families share a shape: a distinguished beginning, then lifespans of implausible length that shorten toward the historical. The Sumerian antediluvian king lists give reigns in the tens of thousands of years; the Hebrew genealogies give lifespans approaching a millennium before a stated limit of one hundred and twenty years; the Vedic yuga scheme places the longest lives in the earliest age. We do not read these as biology. Nor can the numbers be treated as a stable dataset: the king-list figures differ between manuscript recensions and tend to shrink in later copies, and the antediluvian ages in the Masoretic, Samaritan and Greek textual traditions disagree with one another by centuries. Any quantitative treatment of the decline would first have to choose a recension, and that choice would largely determine the result.

What remains debated: What remains debated: whether the longevity pattern is a single inherited schema or independent invention for the same purpose. Prestige inflation in royal annals is well documented and sufficient on its own to generate long reigns at the head of a list. The comparative work that would decide the question does not exist in the form the argument needs: there is no published coded dataset of origin-tradition lifespans with reported inter-rater agreement, and we will not supply figures of that kind. There is also a structural warning from inside comparative mythology. Lincoln's review of Witzel's global synthesis argues that apparent narrative unity across traditions often tracks who wrote the material down — an insider producing a connected account, an outsider assembling an anthology — rather than any property of the traditions [Witzel 2012; Lincoln 2015]. Similarity in this material may be in part an artefact of collection.

Reading: Reading: the Origin Horizon marks a beginning followed by a long interval in which what is known is carried orally, and it is the most weakly anchored era on this site. Stature motifs cluster with longevity motifs — tall ancestors, ancestral giants, a Gilgamesh whose height is given differently in different recensions — and we read them as markers of seniority, of distance, or of ecological memory, not as anthropometry. The value of the material is that it is widely distributed and structurally consistent. The limit is that wide distribution has at least three sufficient explanations — common descent, independent invention for the same social purpose, and the shaping effect of late collection — and the available evidence does not separate them. Coherence is low to moderate. We would rather state that plainly than construct a statistic that appears to settle it.

Source anchors: Henshilwood et al. 2002 Science (engraved ochre, Blombos); Henshilwood et al. 2009 (Blombos ochre series); McBrearty and Brooks 2000 Journal of Human Evolution (the revolution that wasn't); Witzel 2012 The Origins of the World's Mythologies (Oxford University Press); Lincoln 2015 Asian Ethnology (critical review of Witzel)

Tier 2–3 — fossil and archaeological evidence Tier 2, motif comparison Tier 3. Uncertainty high; recension variance alone precludes quantitative treatment of the longevity figures.

What we observe: What we observe: The Greenland ice-core stratigraphy places the onset of Greenland Stadial 1 at 12,896 years b2k and its end at 11,703 b2k on the layer-counted GICC05 timescale, with maximum counting errors of 138 and 99 years [Rasmussen et al. 2014; Walker et al. 2009]. Convention matters: b2k counts from 2000 CE, so the calendar equivalents are 12,846 and 11,653 cal BP; the tighter figure often quoted with these dates is placement precision within the core, not age uncertainty. The widely repeated finding that the change happened within a few years belongs to another quantity again — a one- to three-year shift in deuterium excess, principally a proxy for sea-surface temperature at the moisture source [Steffensen et al. 2008]: where the snow came from, not how cold Greenland was.

On the same cores, the δ¹⁸O transitions that track Greenland temperature are slower and strongly asymmetric — about 60 years at the termination against about 213 years at the onset, with ramp-fitting errors of several decades. The onset was not abrupt in temperature at all. An independent absolute chronology reproduces the asymmetry, uranium-thorium dated speleothems giving an onset at 12,870 ± 30 BP composed of a sharp δ¹⁸O drop of roughly 2‰ within about 20 years nested inside a ~200-year excursion [Cheng et al. 2020]. Magnitudes come from a physically separate method — δ¹⁵N and δ⁴⁰Ar firn thermometry, which reads gas fractionation rather than water isotopes — and are site-dependent: −4.8 ± 1.2 °C at NEEM and −9.2 ± 0.9 °C at GISP2 at the onset [Buizert et al. 2014, uncertainties at two standard deviations].

One result governs how these numbers may be used: the Younger Dryas was some 4.5 ± 2 °C warmer than the preceding Oldest Dryas despite being the more δ¹⁸O-depleted of the two, so magnitudes read off an isotope curve are biased. Regional diachroneity has largely been withdrawn: redating the Laacher See eruption to 13,006 ± 9 cal BP brought European varve chronologies into line with Greenland, and the same ash has since been found in a speleothem record [Reinig et al. 2021; Warken et al. 2025] — though the two studies imply lead times near 199 and 150 years, figures that are not interchangeable. Faunal turnover in North America clusters at this horizon, but the genus count depends on taxonomic and chronological criteria, and the losses are time-transgressive: mammoth persisted on Wrangel Island to about 3,700 radiocarbon years BP.

What remains debated: What remains debated: mechanism. Freshwater forcing — meltwater rerouted from the Laurentide margin, weakening North Atlantic overturning — remains the leading explanation, and it predicts the observed order of events, a moisture-source reorganisation preceding a slower regional cooling [Broecker 2006]. Routing and outlet remain contested, and we adopt no single cause. The formal boundaries are also pinned to deuterium excess, the fastest-switching proxy in the core, which is why the canonical onset looks sharper than the temperature history it dates.

An extraterrestrial contribution is proposed and contested. The Greenland platinum anomaly is real and has been reproduced in North American sequences, where the authors framed it as a time marker rather than as impact evidence [Petaev et al. 2013; Moore et al. 2017]. The discovery paper's own caveats matter: the source cannot be identified, the extraterrestrial inference is called circumstantial, and the inferred impactor 'is unlikely to result in an airburst or trigger wide wildfires'. A volcanic origin fits the anomaly's roughly fourteen-year duration better than an instantaneous event [Green et al. 2025]. Purported nanodiamonds were positively re-identified as graphene and graphene-oxide aggregates present above, at and below the boundary [Daulton et al. 2010, 2017]. On the proponents' own test of isochroneity, 3 of 29 sites fall inside the window [Meltzer et al. 2014], and the 2023 review concluding that the hypothesis should be rejected carries Petaev, author of the platinum anomaly, among its signatories [Holliday et al. 2023].

Reading: Reading: the Younger Dryas onset is disruption before flood — an environmental reversal of known magnitude and reasonably known timing, sufficient to reorganise range and mobility across the northern hemisphere. Its evidentiary weight is unusually well distributed: ice, speleothem, varve and tephra archives now agree within their stated uncertainties, the strongest position anywhere on this site. What none supplies is a cause. We weight the cooling as strong, the freshwater mechanism as moderate and leading, the platinum datum as real but of unresolved origin, and the impact hypothesis as weighing against on the criterion its own proponents proposed. Timing is constrained to roughly a century; cause is not.

Source anchors: Rasmussen et al. 2014 Quaternary Science Reviews (GICC05 stratigraphy); Walker et al. 2009 Journal of Quaternary Science (Holocene GSSP); Steffensen et al. 2008 Science (deuterium excess and transition durations); Buizert et al. 2014 Science (firn thermometry magnitudes); Cheng et al. 2020 PNAS (absolute speleothem chronology); Reinig et al. 2021 Nature (Laacher See); Warken et al. 2025 Science Advances; Broecker 2006 Science (freshwater forcing); Firestone et al. 2007 PNAS (initial hypothesis); Petaev et al. 2013 PNAS; Moore et al. 2017 Scientific Reports (platinum as time marker); Green et al. 2025 PLOS ONE (volcanic alternative); Daulton et al. 2010 PNAS and 2017 Journal of Quaternary Science; Meltzer et al. 2014 PNAS; Holliday et al. 2016 PLOS ONE (blind test); Holliday et al. 2023 Earth-Science Reviews 247: 104502

Younger Dryasice coresplatinummegafauna
Tier 1 strong for the cooling and its timing; Tier 2 for markers. Onset and termination are asymmetric — about 213 and about 60 years in Greenland temperature. Mechanism unresolved; the impact hypothesis weighs against on its own chronological test.

What we observe: What we observe: Between roughly 20 and 7 ka global mean sea level rose by about 120–130 m — not one measurement but a convergence of coral reconstructions and ice-volume inversions [Peltier and Fairbanks 2006; Lambeck et al. 2014]. Because the solid Earth and the geoid respond to the redistribution of ice and water there is no single sea-level curve: every coastline has its own history, and comparison between sites requires an isostatic model whose ice history and mantle rheology are themselves uncertain [Peltier 2004; Peltier et al. 2015]. The robust claim is regional, not global: shelves drowned in a sequence datable locally across some thirteen millennia.

Within that rise, one abrupt pulse is well supported across independent archives. Meltwater Pulse 1A is resolved in the Tahiti drilling record at the Bølling warming about 14,600 years ago [Deschamps et al. 2012] and independently on the Sunda Shelf [Hanebuth et al. 2000]. A second pulse near the close of the Younger Dryas is not in that position. The Tahiti boreholes detect no significant change in the rate of rise across that interval, which the authors read as making such an episode unlikely; their rates are 7.5 ± 1.1 mm yr⁻¹ during the stadial against 12.1 ± 0.6 before and 11.7 ± 0.4 after [Bard et al. 2010]. The paper states its own bound: a step would be masked by uncertainty inherent to the coral method below about 6 m. Tahiti excludes a step of order 15 m; it cannot exclude a smaller one.

The geographies removed are better constrained than the rate at which they went. The Sunda Shelf, up to 800 km wide, stood near −123 m at 20 ka and rose at roughly 10 m per thousand years from 19 to 8 ka; the coastal plains that define the region today grew only across the last 8 to 6 thousand years [Hanebuth et al. 2011]. Exposed-area figures for Sundaland circulate widely and we give none: palaeoshoreline maps at this scale use modern bathymetric contours as proxies, uncorrected for isostasy, tectonics, compaction and sedimentation [Voris 2000]. Modelled marine incursion into the Persian Gulf, mean basin depth about 35 m, reaches the central basin from about 12,500 yr BP [Lambeck 1996], on chronologies whose radiocarbon-against-calendar convention is not consistently clear.

What remains debated: What remains debated: whether a discrete second pulse occurred. Fairbanks's group reasserts it from Barbados reef-crest coral — 14 ± 2 m between about 11,450 and 11,100 yr BP, at rates reaching 40 mm yr⁻¹ [Abdul et al. 2016]. The objections are specific. The cores defining the step come from different reef environments and may sit on different tectonic segments of an actively uplifting island, so the step may be a splice artefact; the indicator species is taken to represent depths less than about 5 m, and the reading requires that tolerance to have been exceeded during rapid rise; and isostatic differences prevent direct comparison with Tahiti [Bard et al. 2016] — an objection cutting both ways, since it also permits a real signal from an Antarctic source whose fingerprint would be large at Barbados and small at Tahiti.

Candidate catastrophes have been revised by their own proposers. The Black Sea breach — catastrophic submergence of more than 100,000 km² at 7,150 ± 100 radiocarbon years BP, roughly 8,000 cal BP once calibrated — was questioned four years later by two of its own co-authors [Ryan et al. 1997; Görür et al. 2001]. Later work finds persistent outflow rather than catastrophic inflow, a lake surface only some 30 m below present rather than 80 or more, and reconnection near 9,000 cal BP in two steps [Aksu et al. 2002; Giosan et al. 2009; Soulet et al. 2011]. An event has been replaced by a process, as with the Storegga tsunami and the end of Doggerland [Walker et al. 2020].

Reading: Reading: the Flood Horizon is the central discontinuity here, and it survives the removal of its most dramatic element — the pulse. The robust signal is a magnitude and a geography: a rise of order 120–130 m, and the loss of highly habitable shelf lands. Flood traditions are wide and patterned, but we give no count: any total depends on how a tradition is delimited. The claim that some Australian traditions preserve postglacial coastal change [Nunn and Reid 2016] has been extended by its authors rather than rebutted in the indexed record, though its dating is circular in form. We weight geographic loss as moderate to strong, the discrete pulse as open, myth coherence as suggestive within limits.

Source anchors: Peltier and Fairbanks 2006 Quaternary Science Reviews (extended Barbados record); Lambeck et al. 2014 PNAS (ice volumes); Peltier 2004 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences and Peltier et al. 2015 JGR Solid Earth (isostatic adjustment); Deschamps et al. 2012 Nature (Tahiti, Bølling); Hanebuth et al. 2000 Science (Sunda Shelf); Bard et al. 2010 Science (Tahiti boreholes); Abdul et al. 2016 Paleoceanography (Barbados reassertion); Bard et al. 2016 Paleoceanography (comment); Hanebuth et al. 2011 Earth-Science Reviews; Voris 2000 Journal of Biogeography (palaeoshoreline maps); Lambeck 1996 Earth and Planetary Science Letters (Gulf shorelines); Rose 2010 Current Anthropology (Gulf basin); Ryan et al. 1997 Marine Geology; Görür et al. 2001 Marine Geology; Aksu et al. 2002 GSA Today; Giosan et al. 2009 Quaternary Science Reviews; Soulet et al. 2011 Quaternary Science Reviews; Walker et al. 2020 Antiquity; Sturt et al. 2013 Journal of Archaeological Science; Korotayev et al. 2006 Journal of American Folklore; Nunn and Reid 2016 Australian Geographer

Tier 1 strong for total rise and regionally dated shelf drowning; Tier 2 for basin reconstructions; Tier 3 for myth coherence. A discrete late pulse is contested, not established: absent from the Tahiti boreholes above their ~6 m resolution, reasserted from Barbados, and challenged on core splicing, indicator depth tolerance and isostasy.

What we observe: What we observe: Göbekli Tepe's occupation spans roughly 9500–8000 cal BC, with the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A phase at about 9500–8700 and the early Pre-Pottery Neolithic B at about 8700–8200 [Clare 2020]. Dating rests on accelerator radiocarbon measurements of charcoal, of organic residues in the mud mortar of the buildings, and of pedogenic carbonate coatings, and the excavators' own caveats should travel with the results: organic material from fill sediments may be older or younger than the structures around it; carbonate coatings accumulate at variable rates and yield average values only; collagen preservation is poor; and a plateau in the calibration curve widens several probability ranges. A wall-plaster determination from Enclosure D gives 9745–9314 cal BC at 95.4 per cent — a four-century interval from one sample. Neither a Bayesian chronological model nor a comprehensive radiocarbon monograph has been published for the site.

Two propositions that circulated widely have been withdrawn by the excavation team. Schmidt's tripartite layer scheme has been abandoned: the round-oval special buildings and the rectangular structures overlap chronologically, and several multi-phase buildings were far longer-lived than previously allowed, with final phases consistent with construction around the mid-ninth millennium cal BC. The reading of the enclosure fills as rapid, ritually motivated backfilling has likewise been replaced. Review of the evidence now points to inundation by displaced archaeological deposits from higher-lying knolls and slopes, which accounts both for the mixed PPNA and PPNB material in the fill and for the heterogeneity of the radiocarbon results; the current model also includes mitigation works undertaken by the prehistoric population to protect the buildings, so it is neither purely natural nor a single deliberate act.

The sanctuary-against-settlement dichotomy has largely dissolved with it. Excavation has produced agglutinated round-oval structures, hearth sequences, bead-production areas, lithics characteristic of domestic contexts, a rock-carved pit some 8.0 m across and 2.8 m deep with bedrock channels and cisterns, a sub-floor burial of at least three individuals, and more than seven thousand plant-processing tools whose phytoliths indicate cereals in quantity [Clare 2020; Dietrich et al. 2019]. The scale of the making remains distinctive. The central pair in Enclosure D stands 5.5 m and weighs on the order of eight to ten metric tons; an unfinished pillar on the plateau runs about 7 m, estimated near fifty tons; the quarries lie on the same limestone within a few hundred metres. Relief carving covers at least ten vertebrate taxa across 22 of 37 pillars, dominated by snake, fox and wild boar; some pillars bear arms and hands in bas-relief, which led the first systematic study to read them as stylised anthropomorphic beings [Peters and Schmidt 2004]. What was eaten — gazelle by count, aurochs by meat weight, both wild and hunted — is largely not what was carved.

What remains debated: What remains debated: nearly everything downstream of the dating. No quantitative workforce or person-hour estimate for the site has been published; the figure of several hundred men moving a megalith over several days, sometimes repeated as a Göbekli calculation, is an Indonesian ethnographic analogy, and we decline to convert it. The estimate of about twenty enclosures and more than two hundred pillars derives from magnetic prospection in 2003, with the project's own caveat that only very large structures register — and, on the revised chronology, those structures were not standing together. Deliberate building-burial has not been abandoned as a regional practice: the excavator at Karahantepe argues that every building excavated there was deliberately filled [Karul 2021]. Whether the special buildings were roofed, and whether a resident population lived on the mound, remain open, and Banning's argument that they were houses rich in symbolic content has gained ground [Banning 2011, 2023].

Reading: Reading: we read Göbekli Tepe as residual expression — planning, quarrying, transport and layout appearing already competent — and the revised chronology requires that claim to be restated rather than repeated. If the monumental and the modest were partly contemporaneous, and if the enclosures were long-lived multi-phase structures rather than sealed episodes, then 'aftermath' cannot carry a temporal sense. The defensible version is synchronic: residual as persisting alongside, not left over after. Nor is the site a monument-before-agriculture threshold in the simple form. The fauna are wild and the cereals show no domesticated morphology, but intensive organised cereal processing predates domestication regionally, and the current literature treats the emergence of farming as protracted rather than as a threshold [Willcox and Stordeur 2012; Asouti and Fuller 2013]. Falsifier: a documented developmental sequence from Epipalaeolithic structures to T-pillar enclosures within a single valley, with intermediate forms, would weigh toward local invention.

Source anchors: Clare 2020 e-Forschungsberichte des Deutschen Archäologischen Instituts (revised chronology; withdrawal of ritual backfilling and of the tripartite layer scheme); Dietrich et al. 2013 Neo-Lithics (radiocarbon sequence); Dietrich et al. 2012 Antiquity (cult and feasting); Dietrich et al. 2019 PLOS ONE (cereal processing); Peters and Schmidt 2004 Anthropozoologica (fauna and iconography); Banning 2011 Current Anthropology and 2023 Open Archaeology; Karul 2021 Türk Arkeoloji ve Etnografya Dergisi (Karahantepe building burial); Özdoğan 2024 Documenta Praehistorica (Sayburç); Kinzel and Clare 2020, in Monumentalising Life in the Neolithic; Willcox and Stordeur 2012 Antiquity; Asouti and Fuller 2013 Current Anthropology; Schmidt 2000 Istanbuler Mitteilungen

Göbekli TepeTaş TepelerPPNAresidual knowledge
Tier 1–2 for dating and architecture. Ritual backfilling and the tripartite layer scheme have been withdrawn by the excavators; the sanctuary-settlement dichotomy has largely dissolved. The residual reading survives only in synchronic form.

What we observe: What we observe: The pillar-and-enclosure grammar of the Urfa plain is not confined to one site. T-shaped uprights are recorded at Nevalı Çori, Karahantepe, Sayburç, Harbetsuvan Tepesi, Sefer Tepe and Kurt Tepesi across the Taş Tepeler cluster, and at Gusir Höyük in the Tigris basin they appear to lack the crossbar. The very large pillars, of four to five and a half metres, remained known only from Göbekli Tepe as of the excavation project's own survey of T-pillar sites. The programme has also transformed the picture faster than the literature: Göbekli Tepe and Nevalı Çori have substantial publication records; Sayburç has two journal outputs, one a short editorially reviewed project report; Karahantepe's international peer-reviewed footprint is thin, its best-known carved pillars press-reported rather than published; several sites remain effectively unpublished.

The closest regional comparanda are informative in a specific way. Nevalı Çori, excavated between 1983 and 1991 and now beneath a reservoir, set pillars of the smaller class inside an unambiguous settlement with a cult building, which is why it long served the Göbekli excavators as their contrast case. At Sayburç the special building stands close to dwellings, and the excavator reads the arrangement as the intertwining of the sacred with everyday life [Özdoğan 2024]. Further south, the Pre-Pottery Neolithic tower at Tell es-Sultan is the standard non-Anatolian comparison; its commonly repeated dimensions — roughly 8.5 m high, about 9 m across at the base, an internal stair of twenty-two steps — come from summaries supplying no radiocarbon basis, and we give them as approximations pending the primary excavation reports.

Atlit-Yam supplies the one direct link between this era and the preceding one: a settlement now underwater off the Carmel coast, with a semicircle of seven megaliths of about 600 kg each bearing cup marks and set around a freshwater spring, and a dry-stone well 1.5 m across and 5.5 m deep whose four use levels end when the water turned saline [Galili et al. 1993, 2004]. It is dated to roughly 8100–7900 BP on charcoal and seeds. The framing caution is substantial: Atlit-Yam is Pre-Pottery Neolithic C, some two millennia later than the Göbekli special buildings, and it is a fishing village. Seven stones of 600 kg attest a standing-stone practice, not a megalithic tradition on the earlier scale.

Astronomical readings have been advanced for both the Jericho tower and for Nabta Playa in southern Egypt, and both warrant distance. Nabta Playa's ceremonial complex belongs to the Late and Terminal Neolithic, roughly 7500–5400 BP, three to five millennia after the Anatolian material; its stellar alignments are advanced by their own authors in hedged terms, as megaliths that may once have aligned with named stars, and have not been independently corroborated [Malville et al. 1998; Malville 2015]. There is also an asymmetry worth naming: the Göbekli excavators reject arguments of exactly this form for their own site, on the grounds that many pillars are not in original positions and were modified and reused.

What remains debated: What remains debated: diffusion against convergence. Within the Euphrates corridor and across a few centuries, shared architectural grammar at a dozen sites is most economically read as one tradition; across the wider Neolithic, and certainly across continents, it is not. Dating compounds the difficulty, since such structures are usually dated from associated charcoal rather than from the stone, leaving centuries of play. One claim can be settled plainly. There is no defensible framing connecting this material to Andean polygonal masonry. Sacsayhuamán is Inca work of the fifteenth century CE, roughly ten and a half thousand years later; it is fitted ashlar in a retaining wall, not free-standing carved monoliths set in sockets; and no mechanism or intermediate distribution has been proposed. That is convergent invention, and we say so rather than leaving a resemblance to do implicit work [Banning 2023].

Reading: Reading: this era is re-settlement and re-expression, and the useful comparison is not size but function. The most productive framing in the current literature holds that monumentality is relational and perceptual rather than a property of dimensions — that what matters is the concept behind a building and how the responsible community perceived it, and that the events inside these structures may have mattered more than the structures [Kinzel and Clare 2020; Watkins 2020]. Read that way, recurrence across unconnected traditions is interesting without implying contact: comparable social problems, independently solved, in the one medium that outlasts flood and fire. Coherence is moderate for regional continuity and absent for intercontinental continuity, and holding that distinction is the whole of the discipline here.

Tier 2 for regional continuity; Tier 1 for the submergence of Atlit-Yam. Publication is uneven across the Taş Tepeler cluster. Any link to Andean masonry is convergent invention, not continuity; Nabta Playa's stellar alignments are hedged by their own authors and uncorroborated.

What we observe: What we observe: Ethnographic and textual records from every inhabited continent retain traditions of intelligent beings understood not to share human substance. Arabian traditions of beings of smokeless fire; Hebrew shedim and se'irim; Zoroastrian daeva and pairika; South Asian yaksha, rakshasa and bhuta; West African aziza and mmoatia; Irish aes sídhe; Diné and Puebloan traditions of shape-changers and ant people; Australian Mimi and Wandjina; Japanese yōkai and tengu; Andean duende. Certain features recur across cases with no plausible contact: a substance distinct from human substance, most often fire, wind, light, smoke or shadow; a parallel society with its own kinship, authority and law; moral agency, so that the beings may be well or ill disposed; the capacity to change form, frequently into named animals; habitation at margins and thresholds — ruins, waste ground, doorways, night markets; and bounded interaction, in the form of affliction, teaching, exchange or abduction.

We give no count of traditions and no measure of similarity. The largest systematic compilation of world folklore motifs is an index organised by motif and area, and any total drawn from it would depend entirely on how one delimits a tradition, a being and a substance category; a bare number would carry an authority it cannot support. The same applies to the distributional claim sometimes made, that fire-substance traditions cluster in arid zones and wind-substance traditions on steppe. Areal-distribution methods capable of testing such a pattern do exist and have been applied to specific motifs with bounded results [Korotayev et al. 2006; Berezkin 2010], as have phylogenetic comparative methods to folktale corpora [Ross et al. 2013; da Silva and Tehrani 2016]. Neither programme has been applied to this material, and both are contested within their own literatures.

The standard readings within anthropology are several and not mutually exclusive: projection of social anxiety; an explanatory model for illness, misfortune and sleep phenomena; a mechanism of social regulation, since the beings enforce the same boundaries people enforce; and, in the Amazonian ethnography, an ontology in which personhood rather than humanity is the widely distributed property and bodies differentiate perspectives. Each accounts for a substantial part of the material. The comparative literature also carries a warning specific to claims of recurrent structure. Lincoln's review of Witzel's global synthesis argues that apparent narrative unity across traditions often tracks the circumstances of textualisation — whether an insider produced a connected account or an outsider assembled an anthology — rather than any property of the traditions themselves [Witzel 2012; Lincoln 2015]. Applied here, the recurrence described above may be in part a property of how the material was collected, translated and edited by comparativists who were looking for exactly such recurrence.

What remains debated: What remains debated: ontology, on which we make no claim. Nothing in this era is offered as evidence that such beings exist. The record is textual and ethnographic, and that record is the whole of what we handle. Among the interpretive alternatives, each has a visible limit. Archetype accounts do not explain why the ascribed substance is so often specified, and specified differently. Readings that treat the traditions as memory of other hominin populations do not account for the shape-changing structure, which is central rather than incidental. Social-regulation accounts explain persistence better than they explain origin. A further difficulty runs through all of them: the traditions were recorded late and mostly by outsiders, which admits feedback between written and oral material — a long-recognised problem in oral historiography that no amount of comparative breadth resolves.

Reading: Reading: the Parallel Horizon is retained here as an interpretive frame rather than a finding — a widely attested body of traditions describing a separate order of beings, whose distribution is broad enough to make single-source diffusion an awkward explanation and whose internal structure is consistent enough to make pure coincidence awkward too. Both awkwardnesses are compatible with several accounts, and we do not choose between them. What the era contributes to the reconstruction is a caution rather than a claim: that widely shared structure is not by itself evidence of shared origin, and that the same reasoning we apply to flood traditions applies here without exception. Coherence is low to moderate. Cultural significance is high, and independent of the ontological question. This is the part of the site where the temptation to overclaim is greatest, which is why the limits are stated at length.

Source anchors: El-Zein 2009 (comparative spirit ontology); Witzel 2012 The Origins of the World's Mythologies (Oxford University Press); Lincoln 2015 Asian Ethnology (critical review of Witzel); Korotayev et al. 2006 Journal of American Folklore (areal distribution of a single motif); Berezkin 2010 Folklore: Electronic Journal of Folklore (motif catalogue and areal method); Ross et al. 2013 Proceedings of the Royal Society B; da Silva and Tehrani 2016 Royal Society Open Science; Viveiros de Castro (Amerindian perspectivism)

parallel orderanthropologyspirit ontologyshapeshifter
Tier 3 — anthropological and textual material, low to moderate coherence. No ontological claim is made or implied. Counts and similarity measures are withheld because both depend on definitional choices.

What we observe: What we observe: Several later traditions display technical precision exceeding evident functional need, alongside explanations of that precision which appear to postdate it. The Great Pyramid at Giza is aligned to the cardinal directions within a few hundredths of a degree, and its base is level to a few centimetres across more than two hundred metres [Spence 2000; Dash 2017]. Both figures depend on decisions about which surviving surfaces define the baseline, and the casing is fragmentary, so the precision quoted is the best-case reading of a damaged monument. The inference sometimes drawn from it — that a particular stellar pair was used for the survey, which would in turn date the method — is a hypothesis reconstructed from the residual error rather than an independent observation.

Mesopotamian sexagesimal arithmetic was used for astronomical prediction with substantial accuracy well before any surviving text sets out its principles, and its place-value notation acquired an explicit placeholder late in its history rather than at the outset. Vedic ritual geometry preserves calendrical structure — year length and intercalation — inside the construction rules for fire altars, transmitted as procedure rather than as theory. In the Andes, fifteenth-century Inca masons fitted polygonal blocks at Sacsayhuamán so closely that the joints admit little more than a blade, without mortar. In each case the operative knowledge is embedded in practice, and the accompanying account of why the practice takes the form it does is either absent or supplied later.

The pattern of interest is the direction of change: earlier examples of a technique showing higher precision and lower stylisation, later examples showing the reverse, with mythic or aesthetic justification expanding as tolerance loosens. One case supplies a control, because its cause is documented. Inca fitted masonry does not continue after the Spanish conquest — not because the technique was mysterious, but because the labour system that organised it was dismantled. Loss of a technique is an ordinary event with ordinary causes, and it is visible here without any inference to a prior high civilisation.

What remains debated: What remains debated: whether any of this requires a residual reading at all, since each case has a plausible local developmental sequence. Egyptian pyramid construction proceeds from Djoser's step pyramid through the Meidum and Bent pyramids to Khufu across roughly a century, with the failures still visible in the record — an ascending series, not an unheralded arrival. Sexagesimal arithmetic has a sufficient origin in administrative accounting. Vedic altar geometry has a sufficient origin in calendrical need, and the institution that transmitted it is well documented. These are strong alternatives and we do not dismiss them. What survives of the observation once they are granted is narrower: that initial competence in several of these traditions appears with relatively few surviving intermediate steps, and is followed by long plateaus in which stylisation increases while precision does not. That is a statement about the shape of the surviving record, and the surviving record is a biased sample of what once existed.

Reading: Reading: Later Ages is thinning — knowledge that was functional becoming symbolic, then decorative — and it is a lens for reading rather than a result. Two limits must be stated. First, the Andean and Old World cases are not connected. The masonry traditions stand roughly ten millennia apart from the earliest material on this site, address different problems with different geometries, and have no proposed mechanism of contact; the resemblance is convergent invention, and we say so rather than allowing juxtaposition to imply otherwise. A popular literature argues the contrary, and the critical replies to it are on record [Banning 2023; Cline 2015; Defant 2017; Shermer 2017]. Second, thinning as described here is compatible with ordinary craft history, in which techniques lapse when the institutions carrying them change — as the Andean case shows directly. The reading is offered because it organises several cases under one description, not because it excludes the alternatives. Coherence is low to moderate. Falsifier: continuous local developmental sequences, with experimental replication for each technique, would weigh toward independent invention throughout.

Source anchors: Spence 2000 Nature (pyramid alignment); Dash 2017 Journal of Ancient Egyptian Architecture (base survey); Neugebauer 1957 (exact sciences in antiquity); Staal 2008 (Vedic ritual and the Agnicayana); Protzen 1993 (Inca stonework); Banning 2023 Open Archaeology (on continuity claims and their popular literature); Cline 2015 American Antiquity; Defant 2017 Skeptic; Shermer 2017 Scientific American

Data Lens

Not proof. A visual account of where independent lines converge and where they thin. Ratings are ordinal judgements with stated bases, not measurements. Select any matrix cell for its reading.

How we weight

Every cluster carries two judgements rather than a score. Evidence is rated limited, medium or robust; agreement is rated low, medium or high. Together they give the ordinal qualifier shown in italics. Tier 1 is measurement (ice-core isotopes, coral uranium-thorium, radiocarbon); Tier 2 is constrained interpretation (stratigraphy, comparative archaeology); Tier 3 is pattern coherence, which is a lens for reading rather than support for a finding. No numeric confidence is published, because a percentage would imply a precision these judgements do not have. Any rating below high states why it was not higher.

Evidence clusters

The Younger Dryas as an abrupt climate reversal

Tier 1

high coherencerobust evidence · high agreement

Three independent archives — Greenland ice, European varves and Asian speleothems — now agree on onset and termination within their stated uncertainties.

Observe
GICC05 places the onset at 12,896 b2k and the base of the Holocene at 11,703 b2k, with maximum counting errors of 138 and 99 years. Firn thermometry gives an onset cooling of −9.2 ± 0.9 °C at GISP2 and −4.8 ± 1.2 °C at NEEM.
Uncertain
Onset and termination are strongly asymmetric, and the cause is unresolved. The often-quoted “few years” figure is deuterium excess, a moisture-source proxy: Greenland temperature recovery took about 60 years and the onset about 213 years.
Would strengthen
Further absolutely-dated archives reproducing the asymmetry between onset and termination.
Would weaken
Evidence that the ice-core boundaries are artefacts of pinning the stratigraphy to the fastest-switching proxy.

Terminal Pleistocene sea-level rise of ~120–130 m

Tier 1

high coherencerobust evidence · high agreement

Coral, sediment and geophysical-model approaches converge on the total magnitude even where they disagree on structure.

Observe
Barbados and Tahiti coral records, Sunda Shelf cores, and the Lambeck and Peltier ice-volume inversions independently support the total rise since the Last Glacial Maximum.
Uncertain
Glacial isostatic adjustment means there is no single global curve. Every site has its own relative history, which is why coral records from different margins are not directly comparable.
Would strengthen
Additional far-field records with independent tectonic constraint.
Would weaken
Systematic revision of the isostatic models underlying the far-field reconstructions.

Regionally dated drowning of continental shelves

Tier 1–2

high coherencerobust evidence · high agreement

The drowning of the Sunda Shelf, the Arabian–Persian Gulf basin and Doggerland is separately dated at each margin.

Observe
Sunda Shelf cores record rapid flooding; Gulf modelling shows progressive inundation from the Strait of Hormuz northward; the Doggerland mapping programme documents staged loss of a large lowland.
Uncertain
Local timing carries larger uncertainty than the global trend. The Storegga slide has been withdrawn by the mapping team itself as the terminal cause of Doggerland's loss.
Would strengthen
Further coring with tighter age control on individual shelf transgressions.
Would weaken
Demonstration that the dated transgressive surfaces are diachronous by more than the models allow.

Meltwater Pulse 1B as a discrete global pulse

Tier 1

low coherencemedium evidence · low agreement

The pulse is present in the Barbados corals and absent from the Tahiti boreholes, and the disagreement is unresolved in print. This is the weakest link in the sequence, and is marked as such.

Observe
Abdul et al. report a rise of 14 ± 2 m at rates reaching 40 mm yr⁻¹ between 11,450 and 11,100 yr BP at Barbados. Bard et al. found no significant change in the rate of rise at Tahiti and considered such an episode unlikely.
Uncertain
Three objections stand against the Barbados expression: cores spliced across different reef environments and possibly different tectonic segments; the depth tolerance of Acropora palmata during rapid rise; and isostatic differences preventing direct comparison. Tahiti excludes a step of about 15 m but cannot exclude one below its own resolution of roughly 6 m.
Would strengthen
An independent far-field archive resolving the interval, or confirmation of an Antarctic source whose fingerprint is large at Barbados and small at Tahiti.
Would weaken
Confirmation that the Barbados step is a compositing artefact between cores requiring different corrections.

Monumental construction preceding agriculture

Tier 1–2

high coherencerobust evidence · high agreement

The sequence itself is well dated; the interpretation placed on it is a separate and much weaker claim, rated below.

Observe
Göbekli Tepe spans roughly 9500–8000 cal BC, with the round-oval and rectangular building traditions now known to overlap. Dating is supported by radiocarbon on organic residues from building mud-mortar.
Uncertain
Schmidt's tripartite layer scheme has been abandoned by the excavation team, and the reading of the enclosures as purely non-domestic no longer holds.
Would strengthen
Further absolute dates from primary building contexts across the Taş Tepeler cluster.
Would weaken
Evidence of a continuous local architectural progression at comparable scale in the same valley.

Reading the enclosures as residual expression

Tier 3

low coherencelimited evidence · low agreement

This is an interpretive reading rather than a finding, and the revised chronology weakens any straightforwardly sequential version of it.

Observe
Sophistication in planning, relief carving and pillar raising appears without a local antecedent at comparable scale.
Uncertain
Absence of an antecedent in the excavated record is not evidence of absence. The overlap of building traditions means the monumental and the domestic are partly contemporaneous.
Would strengthen
A demonstrated technical repertoire that appears fully formed and then measurably thins.
Would weaken
Recovery of developmental phases showing incremental acquisition of the same techniques.

Continuity of pillar traditions beyond the region

Tier 3

very low coherencelimited evidence · low agreement

For distant cases, convergent invention is the defensible reading. No transmission route is evidenced across the intervals involved.

Observe
Upright dressed stones recur across many regions and periods, and within the Upper Euphrates the Taş Tepeler sites form a genuine regional cluster.
Uncertain
Comparisons reaching to Andean masonry span roughly eight thousand years and a hemisphere. Astronomical claims for Nabta Playa are hedged by their own proponents and remain independently unconfirmed.
Would strengthen
Intermediate dated sites along a plausible route.
Would weaken
Formal analysis showing the recurrence is what independent invention would produce.

Longevity and stature motifs as encoded memory

Tier 3

very low coherencelimited evidence · low agreement

Hyperbole is a known feature of king lists, and no count of such traditions is independent of the definition chosen.

Observe
Descending-lifespan schemes recur in Mesopotamian, Levantine and South Asian traditions.
Uncertain
Apparent structural similarity across traditions may be partly a property of how they were collected and edited rather than of the traditions themselves.
Would strengthen
Attestation of the pattern in a tradition demonstrably outside the documented transmission networks.
Would weaken
Demonstration that the scheme is a general property of dynastic list-making.

Comparative spirit ontologies as shared inheritance

Tier 3

very low coherencelimited evidence · low agreement

Recurrence is real; shared descent is not established, and no ontological claim is made here.

Observe
Traditions of intelligent beings of a different substance recur on every inhabited continent, often with recurring attributes.
Uncertain
Recurrence at this level of generality is weak evidence for common origin, and the categories used to compare are themselves scholarly constructions.
Would strengthen
Structural analysis showing the substance mapping is non-random across independent traditions.
Would weaken
Evidence the recurrence follows documented contact and translation histories.

What would change our reading
